and

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t).

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = (2y - 1) \, \mathbf i + (2x - 1) \, \mathbf j.
$$

First, we substitute $x = \sin{t}$ and $y = \cos{t}$ into $\nabla f(x,y)$ to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =(2\operatorname{cos}t-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2\operatorname{sin}t-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(-\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}t-1\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2\operatorname{sin}t-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(-\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}t-1)\cdot \operatorname{cos}t+(2\operatorname{sin}t-1)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}t) \\  & =2{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t-\operatorname{cos}t-2{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+\operatorname{sin}t \\  & =2({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t)+\operatorname{sin}t-\operatorname{cos}t \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}2t+\operatorname{sin}t-\operatorname{cos}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
